utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's my document from May 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Look at item (b).

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: Which one?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: (B), in fact 3(b).

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: The health problem, the local doctor fled, the military doctor is taking charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Who, who is that military doctor?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: The military doctor of my brigade, and we have evidence of that in the protocol of work of my military doctor who provided assistance to many civilians, several dozen, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Look at item (e).

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: There were attempts at theft by military conscripts (jewellery, money) but we responded and the looted items and money were returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Can you explain?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: There were individual cases of attempted theft, but we took very serious and rigorous steps, perpetrators were found in this case, the looted items were taken away from them, returned to the rightful owners, and perpetrators were subject to the required steps.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have a number of documents, but I would like to suggest 5D1083, it speaks of the way of providing supplies and medical assistance; 5D1023, expressing the expectation that humanitarian aid will arrive; and with your leave I would, having said this, move on to another subject.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I would disagree with the categorization of the documents, but I have no objection to the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have Exhibit Number 5D1041, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, is this your document?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's a document of the 37th Brigade, 22nd May 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know approximately how many persons were arrested in your unit and charged with the most serious crimes, such as murders and war crimes?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: There is a clear documentation, Mr. Cepic. As far as I remember for such cases, more than 30 people in the brigade were prosecuted; that is, bad treatment of civilian population and some of them crimes against civilian population. Several dozen members of my brigade were held responsible. That was -- we really made sure to take every step prescribed by our legislation and the international humanitarian law and laws of warfare.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have Exhibit 5D1057, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The exhibit requested was 5D1057.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Look at the heading, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have the second page, please, count 10, also in English probably the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we are waiting for the translation of this document, is it your document?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Look at para 10. Why were these five persons taken into custody?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, these five members of the brigade were taken into custody because there was a well-grounded suspicion that they had committed a series of criminal offences and crimes against the civilian population in Glogovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have 5D1061, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What were these crimes in this one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, those were crimes that resulted from bad treatment of the civilian population, which specific crimes I cannot remember now, but there are records. At this moment I cannot recall the specific crime that these five members of my brigade committed, but it is obvious that they had committed a crime. In fact, there was a well-grounded suspicion that they had and that's obvious from my report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So clarify something you said earlier, were there in fact examples of charges of murder against anyone in your brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, there were members of my brigade charged with murder. I don't know whether this case is one of them, I cannot see that from this report, and I cannot say with certainty whether this is the crime of murder; but there are records of steps taken for murders of civilians and steps were taken of that kind against several members of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We saw a document from April. Now I would like to call up 5D1061. General, is this a document of your brigade? Let's look at the second part [In English] and then again first.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We see the stamp and the signature now?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's an act of my brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Para 5 was requested.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Take a look at item 5, paragraph 2, it begins: "On the 19th of May, 1999," and then some names follow. Can you tell us whether these are members of your unit?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, yes. I stressed a moment ago that there were crimes, and this is one such crime, serious crime, committed against the civilian population. On the 19th of May at around 1800 hours, three brigade members, and the names are stated, wilfully abandoned the unit, went to Kosovo Polje, and killed two civilians. The perpetrators were uncovered and arrested and handed over to the military investigating court in Pristina. According to our information, Bulatovic, who was probably the perpetrator of that act, was remanded in prison and a criminal report filed for murder, and that's what it says in para 5, titled: "Security situation."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, does the name Dusan Mladenovski mean anything to you, is it familiar?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was a member of my brigade, who as far as I remember was also prosecuted for serious crimes against the civilian population, and I think that he -- his name is on the records as having been prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Stevan Jekic is the next person?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Stevan Jekic was also a member of the 37th Brigade and prosecuted for serious crimes, and there's information of individual cases, but I remember this particular case because it was a serious crime. I think that he killed several civilians, a large number of civilians, and the area was in the Gornja Klina-Prekaze-Srbica area, that's where the crime took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there a document relating to that, Mr. Cepic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have some documents, we actually have 5D726, but I spoke with my learned friend before the first session, and I hope that we haven't got any objection now in relation to that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the document is only in B/C/S, however I have received a summary from some of our own staff, so I have no objection for it to be used today in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And this confirms the killing of a large number of civilians, does it, Ms. Carter?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Quite sadistically, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, with your leave, also in Exhibit Number P955, all those names are marked. This is the report from General Vojovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Actually, in that report one name missing, and I will clarify right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, to get through this procedure quicker, I won't open the document, but anyway Slobodan Stosic, Oto Palinkas Igor Mijatovic, Miskic Miodrag, and Bozidar Sudarski, those names?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I have to repeat again. [Interpretation] Slobodan Stosic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, a member of my brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And what post did he occupy in your brigade?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Stosic was the commander of the logistics battalion of the 37th Motorised Brigade, and he was directly subordinated to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Oto Palinkas and Igor Mijatovic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: Oto Palinkas and Igor Mijatovic were members of the logistics battalion of my brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Miodrag Miskovic is the next one?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: Also a member of my brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Bozidar Sudaski?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, a member of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And why were they suspects, General?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, I said that some dozen men were prosecuted. Now, I can't remember the details of each particular case but they were all serious crimes; and I remember the prosecuting of Colonel Stosic, Lieutenant-Colonel Stosic for the killing of civilians in the Srbica-Klina-Prekaze area for a number of crimes of killing of civilians and the battalion commander was prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And these other people, the other names I mentioned?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, these other people also committed a series of crimes and offences against the population. They were uncovered and prosecuted, which shows - and I'd like to stress that - that my brigade paid particular attention to that and something like that wasn't allowed to pass -- go unpunished.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: How about Marko Petric, the next name?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: I think he was a member of the 37th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Milan Rakic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Milan Rakic was a member of the 37th Brigade. He was prosecuted for a killing in the village near Tica, I think the name of the village was Tica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Were there -- was Dejan Djokic there to?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And Mico Racic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was the group of persons prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Miodrag Stosic, was he in the same group?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you and a member by the name of Miodrag Adzic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think he was a member of the 37th Brigade too. And, Mr. Cepic, you have the information and details in front of you. It's easier for you, I really don't have them, so I'm just relying on my memory and of course it's been eight years since then. I do recall that they were members of my brigade, but you mustn't hold it against me if I waiver a bit and take time to think if they were or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: How about Tomislav Milenkovic, the next name?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to remember which crime he was up for?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was killing, murder I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the name Tomislav Milenkovic is in Prosecution Exhibit 955 for crimes of rape under number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, were there other crimes committed, the confiscation of vehicles, theft?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, yes, there were such crimes too in my brigade, and I did emphasise that for all the crimes we learnt about or if we learnt that anybody had committed crimes or offences against international war law and that they behaved badly towards the civilian population were prosecuted. There are a series of documents in the brigade testifying to that. Nobody was allowed or permitted to act in that type of way.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in looking through General Gojovic's testimony and to gain time, P9594, 119, 132, 137, 142, and 144 are persons from the 37th Brigade who committed crimes against property, and also in the other case files, 5955, under number 81.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, the exhibit number is P95 --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: The first exhibit number is P954 and the second one is P955.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, we've heard about Lieutenant-Colonel Stosic, who was immediately subordinated to you. What about other officers, were they replaced for working badly?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cepic, there were cases like that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you give us some specific examples of those, please.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: For failing to implement orders and for the bad situation in the unit, I replaced from duty the commander of the artillery battalion Major Milanovic, as I did -- I also replaced the commander of the 3rd Motorised Battalion, Major Mico Vasic. And I support this once again, Mr. Cepic, and state again that in the brigade strict attention was paid to the functioning of command, and nobody would remain unpunished if they committed bad things. In my brigade, the security chief of the Pristina Corps came by for a time and the corps commander came to visit, as did the army commander, and one of the obligatory questions they asked me during their stay was the soldiers' attitude towards the population and guide-lines and instructions that if there were any transgressions the perpetrators should be punished. And my security organ constantly informed me about the situation in the units, focusing on these issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. That was my last question, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Any Defence counsel have questions? Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I was a bit caught by surprise, but I'll try to organize myself as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General. My name is Branko Lukic.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Branko Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I am Defence counsel for Mr. Sreten Lukic before this Tribunal. I just have a few questions for you. You answered questions about check-points asked -- when my colleague Mr. Cepic asked you and it's Exhibit 5D1031 that I'd like us to look at. It will come up on our screens. And we can see here that mention is made of two mixed check-points. Of the six, four were purely military check-points and under item 3 we can see that an order is being issued within the area of responsibility of each battalion check-points be set up at the entrance and exit to the zone, to the area. I don't know whether this was explained, but I'd like to ask you this: All these check-points are on roads, are they, on communication lines?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, no, that's not quite true. They weren't all on the roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what I was not clear about. So could you explain the situation to us.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the check-points - and from this order we can see that - the check-points are set up -- are being set up and then it says "mixed check-point" too. So let me differentiate between those two concepts. A check-point means that you have an element of combat deployment for a battalion, for lower units, by which immediate security is provided, that is to say it provides the elements needed for its deployment. It need not be an a communication line, on a road, but it must be along the combat deployment line of a battalion in order to provide security. Now, mixed check-points are set up on important roads and communication lines which enter the zone or exit the zone, so approach roads or exit roads, and those need not be directly linked to the unit. At these mixed check-points, you are able to control the movement of the population and the movement of soldiers and anybody else in the area; and that's how they were conceived in the first place. And manning the mixed check-points you would have members of the military police, the army, and members of the Ministry of the Interior, with clearly defined powers and authorisations. The members of the Ministry of the Interior would control civilians and everything that did not belong and come under the army, whereas the members of the military police of the army would exert control over military personnel, soldiers, NCOs, commanding officers, vehicles, and so on and so forth. I don't know if I've managed to explain it properly to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, General, you have. Thank you. Now, you also spoke about Izbica. I don't know what the witness scheduling is for General Lazarevic, the Lazarevic Defence, but I'd like to take advantage of your knowledge and experience for those moments when you were in the Izbica area and ask you about that. Your neighbour to the west was the 7th Infantry Brigade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, do you know that this infantry brigade in the area of Izbica village engaged in anti-terrorist actions on the 12th of April, 1999; for example, on the 15th of April, 1999; the 10th and 11th of May, 1999; as well as the 28th of May, 1999?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the 7th Infantry Brigade was my neighbour on the right, but as of the time when it arrived in Kosovo it was to my right. And I emphasised previously, I think we dealt with this matter earlier on, that they were engaged in action. We even acted together in certain actions. I don't remember the dates that you quoted, but I do know that activities were undertaken in their area and that was their area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you know whether the terrorist forces in those actions suffered any losses?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly, yes, they did, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to ask you something else. A document which is on e-court under 6D1473. We don't have a translation for this one, so I will ask you to read for us three sentences and give us a brief comment. In the first paragraph, the second line, could you begin with the words: "Does on the day of ..."

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you clarify that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the first paragraph. You can read the whole first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: I see it. "Does on the 14th of April, 1999, a group of two to three terrorists disguised in VJ uniforms stopped a MUP vehicle on the road from Orlate village towards Malisevo and killed one member of the MUP and wounded another one, the commander of the police station in Malisevo."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the top of the document, please, and the bottom of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's a document of the 37th Motorised Brigade, right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know if there were other abuses of the VJ uniform by both the police and the KLA?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is not the first case, but it's a dramatic one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will have to repeat the question; it is not recorded correctly. I actually asked: Do you know that there happened abuses of police and VJ uniforms by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In para 6 of this order, in response to the situation on the ground, could you read that para 6?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: "Provide for adequate 'marking' of brigade members with red bands or armbands that will be requested and provided in the sufficient number by the Pristina Corps logistics command. These bands will be worn in the way that will be explained and ordered and occasionally changed. All persons who do not have these or who do not wear them in the prescribed way for that day shall be taken into custody to the command post of the battalion or artillery battalion."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Those have been all my questions for you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just one intervention. I think that there is no -- my question whether this order was enforced in practice, and I think the witness answered yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: May it please the Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: General, you indicated that you first came into Kosovo on 7 -- or around 7 March of 1999; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the beginning of March 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: The reason I ask is because there has been indication in this case that there was a plan in 1998 by the name of Grom 98, and it was under Exhibit 4D140, and specifically it engages your unit within the first phases at point 3.2 in allegedly July of 1998. Was your unit in Kosovo in 1998?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: No, my unit was not in Kosovo in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Did you ever receive any sort of call-up order or any indication that you were being contemplated for engagement in 1998?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: I really don't remember receiving that kind of call-up or indication. There certainly existed a plan of use of the army, and within that plan, plans have been developed for using lower-ranking units. I had no access to plans of high-ranking commands. It is possible that we had been in the plan for being used in that area. I cannot tell you specifically.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: All right. So it's safe to say that only in the few months in 1999 was the 37th Motorised Brigade ever in Kosovo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, early in March 1999 we arrived in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. When you first arrived, what was your unit tasked to do specifically?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean the beginning of March 1999? That period?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Carter, my unit in that period carried out combat training intensively, focusing on drills in order to train as a unit for specific tasks. It was intensive training. That's what we were engaged in in that period.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When you say you were in intensive training, where and in what manner?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: Part of the training took place within the barracks and another part of the training was outside of the barracks. Those were mostly exercises that cannot be organized and carried out within the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Where were those barracks located?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: The barracks was in Kosovska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: At what time did your engagements change?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: My engagements changed dramatically when the war was declared, when the state of war was declared. I believe that's the period when it changed, but I don't know which changes specifically do you mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Let us call up Exhibit P2039, and specifically to the page 3 of the English and page 2 of the B/C/S. This is an engagement order from 20 March of 1999 that you discussed with Mr. Cepic a bit, and you indicated at that point that at page 5, line 4, that over the course of regular combat activities there were unprovoked attacks on your unit. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of conducting exercises in the beginning of March, in the area of exercise Siptar terrorists attacked my unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: However, I would indicate to you on number 14 that's in front of you where it says the main tasks for the next day were for you to continue to carry out the planned offensive action in accordance with the Pristina Corps commander's order strictly confidential 455-44 that began on 19 March, 1999. If there were planned offensive attacks weren't you already attacking the KLA?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: While we performed these exercises, we were subject to attacks by Siptar terrorist forces. We had two options: Not to engage in exercises, to return to our barracks and do nothing; the other option was to defend ourselves, that is, to remove the threat. And those activities were geared at removing the threat posed by terrorists by fighting them.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: In the orders that you received from the Pristina Corps, were exercises oftentimes quantified as planned offensive actions?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Carter, you are engaged in an exercise and you are being attacked from all sides, you have to counter-attack. To move in to counter-attack as a follow-up, it's no longer an exercise, you begin fighting terrorists to survive; in order to survive, you have to fight. We had no intention originally to fight terrorists in the beginning of March. Our intention was to carry out military exercises and to improve our combat-readiness, but from the moment when our unit was attacked, we had to respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter, do we have the order 455-44?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, not that I'm aware of, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: However, your exercises not only began a planned offensive operation -- excuse me, actions on 19 March, it also produced a command post in the general area of Galica village. How often did your combat exercises require a command post?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: Can we see the date when this command post was established in Galica village?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I possess only this document.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: I would just like to see the top of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: If we can move to page 1, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's already the 20th of March.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Now we'll move to the --

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: So it -- sorry to interrupt you, Ms. Carter. To command the unit there must be an organization exercising command, that organization has to have a place from which it exercises command; that place is called command post. It's a location from which the unit is commanded, both in peacetime and in wartime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When did you establish your command post, Mr. Dikovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in this specific case on the 20th of March. We see that from the report. I'm informing the commander of the Pristina Corps that I set up a command post in the area of Galica village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you saying, though, that from the 7th of March you would require to have a command post outwith barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, a command post is positioned in the most favourable location for successful exercise of command. Normally it is in the same place where the unit is. In smaller units, it can be within the battle order. So to command units, a command post has to be set up, from which units are commanded. The command post consists of the commander, part of the staff or part of the operations officer, depending on the specific command post, and the security, support detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Between the 7th of March and the 20th of March, on how many occasions did you establish a command post for the purpose of your combat training exercises?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot recall exactly, but I believe twice prior to this date, prior to the 20th of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I'd also like to direct your attention to item 8.4 in this same order, that would be page 2 in the English and page 2 in the B/C/S. 8.4 indicates that combat group 37 is engaged in suppressing terrorism along the Balinci village-Ljubovac village-Poljance village axis from 20 March 1999 on the orders the Pristina Corps commander strictly confidential Number 445-44 of 19 March 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could we have page 1 in B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, what's your question, Mr. -- or your submission, Mr. Cepic?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I believe I had the wrong page in the B/C/S, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It looks like you have the right page, but perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, I again pose to you if the 37th was engaged in suppressing terrorism along this axis, how are you quantifying that as combat exercises?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Carter, the 37th Brigade was not engaged in suppressing terrorism at that moment on that axis. At that moment, on that axis, part of the 37th Motorised Brigade was engaged in suppressing terrorism, namely, Combat Group 37, not the brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now would you answer the question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please repeat the question, Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the question is how can you say that you were engaged in exercises when your report is that you were engaged in suppressing terrorism in accordance with an order from the Pristina Corps command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Carter, in the area of Kosovo I did not arrive with my combat group to fight terrorists; we were engaged in exercises. However, from the moment when the terrorists attacked us, when I reported to the commander of the Pristina Corps about these attacks, I received orders from the Pristina Corps commander to fight those terrorists.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I've had indication from our case manager that, in fact, we do have the document that's referred to, that 455 order. Unfortunately, it is not in e-court as of now, it will be shortly, if the Court would like to peruse that over the lunch break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I'd now like to move on to P2031, that's the Joint Command order 455-54.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I would ask you to familiarise yourself with this and orient yourself because shortly I'll be asking you to use a map in order to describe what the actions actually took place under this order. Please tell me when you're ready.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I would like to bring up the Kosovo atlas Exhibit Number P615, at pages 17 and 18, and for ease of the witness I do have a --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: The witness saw just the front page, nothing more than the front page, so if my learned friend has got hard copy in B/C/S that would be probably useful.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: That is exactly what I'm tendering right now. And if possible we'd like to focus in on column F, the bottom three sectors on page 17; and column G, the bottom three sectors on page 18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The other way, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: If we could match the resolutions. The bit to the right has much larger grid lines than the one to the left in order to line this up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, don't change them anymore. Just leave them the same size. Now, is that too high, Ms. Carter? Is it further down you want to be?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yeah, it's the bottom --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's the bottom row and that size is fine. Still further to go. We should see the whole of the bottom one. That's it. And do the same on the left. That's it. I hope this is worth it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, can you please tell me based on this Joint Command order where both your unit as well as all of your coordinated and subordinate units were placed on this grid, if you can mark that on the screen.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. On this map the area is not shown. I cannot show you because it's not seen here, it's not visible on this map.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, the map that's on the screen now is enlarged a bit too much. I need the three bottom sectors in order to show this entire operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, while the map is being looked for, it may be my oversight, but I believe the witness gave a clear answer concerning orders with the heading "Joint Command." He said that in his mind those were orders of the Pristina Corps; however, my learned friend, Ms. Carter, says on orders of the Joint Command. It sounds a bit different to me compared to the testimony of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is an area there's a dispute about, and the Prosecution position is quite clear, that this says it's a Joint Command decision and they are proceeding on the basis that it does what it says on the tin. That's a matter we're going to have to resolve in due course when you've made all your submissions.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: General, are you now able to identify the locations at issue in this order on the maps?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Carter, I'm trying to do my best, but I'm sorry that I can't do it yet. Now, to help you out, provide me with the part of the map showing Kosovska Mitrovica, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: That should be the -- well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's in a different -- entirely different place. We must be at --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, actually --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- cross-purposes here.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: -- If we showed the fourth quadrant at the top of

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: in order to show the bottom three sectors.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Do you see -- okay.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And if I can move the map to match again. If we can only move the right one. The right-hand one. We need the bottom three --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're moving the left one. We need to move the right one, apparently, although I'm finding it difficult to understand at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: For assistance, if I were to hold out to you that on the left-hand of your screen, if you were to look to the third box to the top, the one at the very top, you have Runjak is almost in the middle of that quadrant.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: You're talking about the left-hand side, are you?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: Runjak.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: I do apologise, but I can't find it on that left-hand side of the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is this -- this is a name we haven't had yet. Are you talking about Vranjak.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I'm saying Runjak because it actually is a position that's noted in this order. I just thought it would be for ease of the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the left-hand side of the map, I really can't find that feature, and looking at the left-hand side of the map again, I can claim that I wasn't there with almost absolute certainty; and I'm talking about the left-hand side of the map, it's got Srbica, Istok, and Klina, and in that area on the 22nd of March, I was not there.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: If that is what you're seeing, then we clearly do not have the correct page?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is now 12.43, perhaps if we could break a few minutes earlier and if I can work with the registry in order to have this brought up immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You can surely see what's on the screen just as -- I mean, they are pages 5 and 6 of the Kosovo atlas if that's what you wanted to bring up.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: However, we shall interrupt and let you try to sort it out. Mr. Dikovic, we have to have a break again at this stage. Could you please leave the courtroom with the usher and we will see you again in an hour at 1.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.44 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, in an effort to close out the topic of the P2039, the orders from 20 March of 1999, Mr. Reid actually located the document on our system and we have now uploaded in e-court P3049, that's a Joint Command order for Kosovo and Metohija bearing the confidential number 455-44, engaging the troops at the request of General Dikovic, and we would like to use that document now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well -- sorry, Mr. Cepic, do you have some objection to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is the first time we've seen this document, so under Rule 68 my objection is that it should have been disclosed to us earlier. It has to do with the activities of the army in the period covered by the indictment or under Rule 66. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that was done on 18 January 2007.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We're told it has been disclosed almost a year ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have this information, neither do my colleagues, so I would like to express my reservations in that sense. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It is directly related to a document which arose in your own examination-in-chief, and to fully understand it, it's clearly in the interests of justice that we should see this document also, so we shall allow it to be used in the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: General Dikovic, I would first like to draw your attention to the introduction portion of this document, specifically that this is a document from the Joint Command of Kosovo and Metohija dated 19 March of 1999, and it relates back to your combat report P2039. You had indicated before that you believed you were only involved in exercises at that time; however, I'd like to draw your attention to portion 4.3, which is on page 4 of the English and page 3 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I see Mr. Cepic on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my learned friend said that the General said that he only participated in exercises, but when asked directly by me whether he participated in the action he confirmed that he had and we referred to the same paragraph that my learned friend is referring to. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter, is that your recollection of the evidence?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Quite clearly we were discussing how 2039 contemplated exercises, when it quite clearly contemplated combat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think the question is in order in the circumstances, so please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can show 4.3 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, this indicates that as of 19 March of 1999, that the 37th Motorised Brigade with PJP units in Kosovska Mitrovica and Pec participated in combat operations. How do you explain this Joint Command order sending you into combat with your earlier testimony that you were merely being brought in to do training and exercises?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Carter, I did not say that I thought I was participating in exercises; I clarified up to what point the combat group carried out exercises and from what point on combat with Siptar terrorist forces began. I have no doubts in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's understand one another. It may be due to linguistic misunderstandings. This order which is of the 19th, it says combat-readiness on the 20th and it refers to actions which were to take place on the 20th of March. The Prosecutor, as far as I can tell, in -- on page 72, line 3, she mentions the 19th of March; however, it's not the 19th but the 20th of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The order is dated the 19th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but in the previous document we see combat-readiness on the 20th of March at 5.00 a.m. We can't have both on the same day. So we are referring now to the 20th of March. That's all I wanted to point out now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Respectfully, Your Honour, number 14 of 2039 it indicates continued to carry out the planned offensive and with the order of the 19th of March; that's where the date came in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The document we're looking at, though, is P3049; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Then when is it then, Mr. Dikovic, you say that your involvement changed from training to combat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the course of conducting exercises, there were attacks by Siptar terrorist forces, fierce attacks, on the unit and in the area where I was conducting exercises. I regularly informed the commander of the Pristina Corps about these activities of the Siptar terrorist forces. He decided that combat with the terrorist forces should be organized because there were really strong terrorist forces in that area controlling the roads, launching constant attacks on the unit, and there was no other option. The roads had to be deblocked and the area had to be put under control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So when were you given orders to engage directly in combat rather than simply to respond in self-defence, if necessary, during training operations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I cannot recall the precise date, but in the documents, or rather, in the order issued by the Pristina Corps commander the date exists, it has to be there precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we shall read your evidence obviously very carefully to see if, in fact, that was the indication you gave us earlier. Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Respectfully, Your Honour, on that note I would point both the Court as well as the witness to his response at 5.4 -- I'm sorry, page 5, line 4 with regard to the original document P2039, he was presented with a question by Mr. Cepic with response coming: "Yes, Mr. Cepic, 8.4 I can see. I said a moment ago in the course of performing our regular combat activities there was a totally unprovoked attack by terrorists."

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Dikovic, what I would propose to you is: How can the terrorists have an unprovoked attack when your unit was already involved in combat operations directed at them?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Carter, an unprovoked attack took place while exercises were being conducted by my unit in the general area of Kosovska Mitrovica. So I was conducting regular activities on an area designated for such activities, I was doing exercises, and I suffered an attack by terrorists. I repeat, those first terrorist attacks on my unit were totally unprovoked. What their aim was they know better than I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And, sir, I would also like to question you about the title of this document, that it's coming from the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija. You spoke repeatedly during direct examination of how you do not recognise this command body, yet you've had repeated orders starting on 19 March 1999, when your combat operations began, from this body. How do you explain that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Carter, I denied the existence of a Joint Command because for me, for my combat group, and for the 37th Brigade it did not exist because I received orders exclusively from the commander of the Pristina Corps. Why it says "Joint Command" on the document I don't know. I never saw that command. I saw exclusively and carried out tasks exclusively under the command of the Pristina Corps commander. I beg you to understand this because I've had more than one question about this and there is no other answer I can give. It was the Pristina Corps exclusively that was in command of my unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: In 4.3 it's also contemplated that the PJP units will be involved in the same operation. Would you agree with General Delic's assessment that the reason these documents say "the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija" is because it binds not only the Pristina Corps but also the MUP forces?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know, Mrs. Carter, what General Delic said this -- said here, but I know that I personally asked General Lazarevic, Who is my commander, you or this Joint Command, as written here? I received an explicit answer, I am your commander and you are under the command of the Pristina Corps. I got another confirmation of this, talking to Colonel Radojko Stefanovic, who came from the command of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When did these confirmations come?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: As soon as I received an order with the wording "Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija." I got an explanation from Colonel Stefanovic that this is because of the coordinated action and cooperation with MUP forces. I was quite satisfied with that explanation and my mind was put at rest. Finally when I heard from my commander, You are under my command. My unit was part of the Pristina Corps, and it was logical for me to ask: What kind of Joint Command is this now? And I was persistent until I got a satisfactory reply. From that moment on, only that command existed for me, the command of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Now, you've indicated the Joint Command was in reference to joint operations with the MUP, so are you saying that if it was an order that only dealt with the VJ it was entitled "Pristina Corps"; and if it was an order that involved both the police and the VJ, then it would say "Joint Command"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's a misrepresentation of what the witness said, because my learned friend says in the first part of her question: "You've indicated the Joint Command was in reference to joint operations with the MUP -- [In English] Joint operations with the MUP," [Interpretation] Whereas he explained not about the Joint Command but the what the document represents, that's in my humble opinion. I don't believe this question is well-founded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is it you say that is an inaccurate representation of what the witness has said?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, my learned friend says that the Joint Command exists. She doesn't say, This is the wording on the document; she says -- she uses the name of the Joint Command and that's not how the witness answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It seems very difficult for you to understand, Mr. Cepic, that when an expression which so many of your witnesses are having difficulty in explaining clearly to the Court exists, that it's appropriate for the Prosecution to test the issue of its definition with all the witnesses who speak about it. I do not see any misrepresentation in the question that's been asked, and it's not obligatory at this stage for the Prosecution to accept that there was no such thing as a Joint Command. It may be after the judgement's rendered, that remains to be seen. But at this stage in time they have a basis for submitting to witnesses that such a body existed, and that's what they are doing and inviting comment on. Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you. And in order to provide General Dikovic with a basis.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your answer when I asked you about confirmations was that: "As soon as I received an order with the wording 'Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija,' I got an explanation from Colonel Stefanovic that this is because the coordinated action and cooperation with MUP forces," so what I'm asking you if it was an operation that dealt with VJ only, did that bear the title "Pristina Corps," while joint operations with the MUP would bear the moniker "Joint Command"?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: I really could not distinguish quite well between the two. I cannot make such conclusions, because in my mind the command of Pristina Corps was my superior command at all times, and they commanded me, no Joint Command, and I sent my reports to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I wonder if you'd think of it -- that question very carefully. It's a very good question in the overall context of this case, whether that might be the distinction, that it was an operation or action, rather, where only the VJ were involved, the heading on the order or decision might be different. Now, could you think about that. If you can't answer it, obviously we understand because we're asking you to remember a large number of documents. But is that a possible explanation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, until the very end of the war I received orders to cooperate with MUP forces and I performed jointly with them some of my tasks throughout the war, regardless of whether the heading read "command of the Pristina Corps" or "the Joint Command." I did not understand that there was a clear distinction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you'll understand our anxiety about this whole matter, that you cannot, in spite of being a member of a body whose affairs are carefully regulated, cannot give any indication to us of the circumstances in which the heading would be "Joint Command" in the document and the circumstances in which the heading would simply be "Pristina Corps command." It doesn't do just to dismiss it as some sort of aberration because there is some sort of pattern to this and that is what we're trying to find.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I really did not analyse these documents that would enable me to conclude "Pristina Corps" covers such and such actions, whereas another type of actions goes under "Joint Command," because in my mind there was always only one thing, the command of the Pristina Corps. I did not have command in my area over MUP forces; they were under the command of their own superiors along the chain of command of the Ministry of the Interior. We often cooperated and acted in coordination, but each body commanded its own forces. It never occurred once that I commanded MUP forces or vice versa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, can you please describe for us then, when you were tasked on the 20th or the 19th of March, 1999, with this joint action with the PJP units in Kosovska Mitrovica and Pec, can you please describe how those operations worked.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Carter, could you phrase the question more specifically? What do you mean how the operations worked?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I'll direct your attention to paragraph 4.3 which is on your screen and it's discussing this operation with PJP units. What I would like to know is how that operation worked. Who was commanding? What were the results? How did the reporting work? Can you please just describe for us how that first operation worked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't object to the question, but something about the earlier question. It -- just [indiscernible] from this English transcript that the operation was in Kosovska Mitrovica and Pec, but if you read the document it says that the PJP companies are from Kosovska Mitrovica and Pec. Just look at the first line of paragraph 4.3. Mrs. Carter seems to read this as the operation taking place in Kosovska Mitrovica and Pec, unless I'm mistaken. I just believe it's better to clear this up, otherwise please forgive me, Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fila. I think, Ms. Carter, you'll find that the areas where the action was undertaken was set out after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'll be more precise in my language.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, there's a specific axis that's noted in the third line of this 4.3. Can you please describe when did your units as well as the PJP units arrive to this axis?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Carter, I really cannot remember the exact time, you'll find it in my reports. I believe you have access to them. I really cannot give you the exact time when they arrived. You must appreciate that I can't remember. Do you recall what you had for breakfast seven days ago or where you were sitting when you had breakfast?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, my breakfast is not relevant; however, you did testify quite distinctly on P2039 which is your report, in which you said you continued to carry out the planned offensive. If that offensive was ordered on the 19th I want to know when exactly did your units arrive along with the PJP units for combat operations?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down for interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry about mentioning breakfast, but I hope you'll understand. At that time I had my report in front of me; now I have the order of the commander of the Pristina Corps before me. It's easier for me to look at my report.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I'd like to provide a hard copy of P2039 in B/C/S for the witness's ease.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, when did your units arrive along with the PJP?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: 20th and 21st of March.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And when all of -- and when all of the forces arrived, who was coordinating the operations on the ground?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Carter, everyone commanded their own forces, thus my combat group commander commanded the Combat Group 37. Commanding officers of PJP units commanded their own units. In the field synchronization took place between us and axes of attack were defined to determine exactly along which axis which unit shall attack. That was necessary because I needed to know where the attack is being launched by PJP units and so that they should know along which axis we are going to attack. That step must be taken in every operation because if that is not done friendly fire can occur and result in great losses. Coordinated action, therefore, and cooperation in terms of time, place, and method of carrying out the assignment. Army units are commanded by the army; MUP units are commanded by the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And when you arrived with the PJP units and any other subordinated units at the time, approximately how many terrorists were you fighting?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Carter, I can tell you this: There was a large number of terrorists. I did not count them, but judging by the fire and by the fierceness of the attack against my unit and police units, there must have been many. I couldn't count them; if I could have, I wouldn't have been able to fight them. They were in shelters, in trenches, in houses, and they opened fire from everywhere --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, the reason I --

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: That's why I cannot tell you precisely --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And the reason I ask that is I'm trying to figure out at what point does it become appropriate to use six T-55 tanks? And this is your unit alone.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: If the terrorists fire from fortified [Realtime transcript read in error "45"] buildings that they had prepared in advance and they used, in particular, basements and lower floors because they provided the best cover, if they were firing from trenches and bunkers previously prepared, we could and we did use tanks to destroy those firing points. Only in those cases when it was necessary to destroy terrorists who are fortified and cannot be neutralised with rifle fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: However, nowhere --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, just one error in transcript, page 82, line 9, witness didn't say fortified buildings.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The witness did say "fortified" buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: In Serbian [B/C/S spoken].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: "Fortified," but it has been --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Exactly, exactly, fortified, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But it's been transcribed as "45."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, if the concern is that these were fortified buildings and exist, would it be fair to say that oftentimes these were populated villages?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: In part, yes, yes. They were also in villages and how; unfortunately, they were in villages and that was no accident, no accident. They knew, they knew that the army would not shell villages, that civilians were there, that civilians were a shield for them. I only wish they were not positioned in villages, but they were and how.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And we've heard many witnesses testify prior to you that in the event that you're dealing with a populated place it was the duty of the VJ and the MUP to remove the civilians from the area of combat prior to those operations taking place. I want to know when or if you actually moved the civilians out of these locations.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Carter, we did not move them, we did not move them. Civilians left of their own accord. We did not move them. How would you move civilians out of a village in which terrorists are positioned? How could you approach the village and say, You civilians get out and you terrorists stay so that we can fight you? It doesn't work that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Six T-55 tanks would probably do it for me to leave. Do you not account for the fact -- because you testified previously that you think the only reason civilians were moving out of the area was because of the KLA and NATO. NATO was not even involved at this point. The only people that were involved is the VJ, the MUP, and the KLA. Do you not see how six T-55 tanks might produce movement of the population?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Carter, if my memory serves me well, I said that but it was in response to a question that related to the period after the 20th [as interpreted] of March --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: After the 25th of March --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- after NATO air-strikes started. I said that in response to Mr. Cepic, who asked me about the 25th of March and later.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: However, the indictment period that's in issue begins in January of 1999. What we're trying to find out is why these civilians were already on the road. Can you explain to me what care was given to the civilians when producing this Joint Command operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, could we have a reference to those civilians on the road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that that's an inherent part of this question. The question relates to what was done about the civilians at the various villages where this action on the 20th and 21st of March was being undertaken. Can you deal with that, please, Mr. Dikovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 20th until the 21st of March, if my memory serves me well - and it should be in documents - on the axis of attack of my forces there were no civilians. That's the 20th and the 21st of March. I didn't see any.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Then we'll move on to the next operation that was on the 22nd of March, and that's at P2031. I had given you a copy of that order before we broke, and then I would like to call-up Exhibit P3050.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I would like to make a note that P3050 are two excerpts from the Kosovo atlas, which is P615 which was shown in e-court previously, and it's pages 17 and 18 that have directly been placed side by side. The first page shows a full view of the original pages from the atlas and the second page shows a zoomed-in view of the sectors and the centers we were trying to do before the break.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The counsel is kindly asked to slow down for the translators.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, under the Joint Command order P2031 of 22 March 1999, can you please look at this map -- I've given you both hard copies for ease of reference but we'll be doing some markings on the screen itself in order to make notations of where you were located and how this operate proceeded. Have you been able to orient yourself on to the maps?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I see it. I see the maps and I have it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And to begin, if the order was drafted on 22 March of 1999, at what point did your units engage?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: I did not understand you. At what point were they engaged? Could you clarify?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Well, there's been some confusion, if the order was drafted on the 22nd, when did you act on that order and go into this location?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: As a rule, the order of the 22nd was not implemented on the same day. Implementation took place over the following days. From the moment an order is received until the commencement of implementation, preparations were done. So receipt of an order from the superior command does not immediately trigger implementation. The order probably specifies at what time troops have to be ready. That's usually indicated in para 4, and it is that moment that marks the commencement of implementation. That's when I move.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And as this is an action that was ordered just prior to the NATO bombing campaign, I want to know what preparatory actions were taken at that time.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: You mean preparatory actions for this operation, that's what you mean, Ms. Carter?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: Upon receiving the order, upon receiving the order, the following activities were carried out, if I remember well: Observing the objects of attack, that is, assessing the Siptar terrorist forces at my own level because before performing the assignment I had to determine where the Siptar terrorist forces were located. I had to assess, at least approximately, the strength of their forces and where they were. I had to issue assignments to my units and I had to establish full cooperation with the MUP, as I described earlier. Those are the preparations for carrying out operations as a rule.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And these operations were going to take place in Izbica, just near Srbica, Padalista, and a number of other villages. What, if anything, was done with the population who resided in those villages prior to the commencement of the operation?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Carter, I cannot answer this question, Izbica, Padalista, and the other villages because I believe my unit was not on that axis at the time. If you look carefully at the order you will see that we were not going towards Izbica or towards Padalista.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What -- which villages was your company or your unit going to be taking?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Carter, we were not supposed to capture any of the villages. We were not supposed to attack the villages. It was not our task to take control of villages. Our task was to destroy the Siptar terrorist forces. Our objective was not the village; our objective were Siptar terrorist forces, no villages. These villages are listed here as features for easier orientation. If I tell you Padalista village, you will know immediately where I am, in which area; it doesn't mean that I'm in the village. So we were not attacking villages. We attacked Siptar terrorist forces. And if they were in the village or put up resistance from the village, inflicting losses and such things happened, such cases happened, we had to neutralise that, because it was our objective, our target. If he is putting up resistance from a building, it's a legitimate target; if he's opening fire on me from a building, it's a legitimate target. Ms. Carter, I cannot just put up my hands and say you are firing from a building so I'll wait till you get out, and then we'll see, we'll fight then, to put it literally.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You said you've already done reconnaissance, you've checked the area, then it's time to go in. Apparently your command post was in the village of Krasalic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, the village of Kraznic was not my command at the time. Let me take you back to my report at the time where I said where I was. I can't recall exactly where now, but I'm sure my command was not in the village of Krasnic because I know approximately where that village is.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I'm sorry my accent may be getting in the way. I said Krasalic that is in section 5.2 of the joint command order, just before 5.3 which indicates that your command post was going to be in the village of Krasalic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: I have to take you back to the order -- to the report again. Whether it was in the village of Krasalic -- well, you see, it wasn't in the village. For me to set up my command in the village of Krasalic, the village would have to be abandoned. How could I do that in the midst of civilians? It wasn't the village of Krasalic, the houses in the village, it was only in the general area in the village of Krasalic, not in the village itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, will you please go to 5.2 and read the final line that is talking about your command post and will you please read it for the record.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't have it before me.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it was apparently removed. It was P2031, look at 5.2 and look at where your command post was to be set up.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but in the area of the village of Krasalic. It doesn't say in the village of Krasalic, I'm reading. It says a command post in the area of the village of Krasalic, area, that's a broad concept, it has its depth and its surface area --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, can you please just read the line as it's written on the page.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: "Command post in the area of the village of Krasalic."

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: How close were you to the village?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: I was close enough to be safe from the Siptar terrorist forces, that's how close I was to the village. I was certainly in the area of the village. Where was I in the area of the village? In the most favourable place from which I could monitor the combat deployment of my units and to see where they are. You couldn't do that from the village. When you get into a village, you see 15 or 20 houses around you, you don't see the terrain. You can't have a command post in a village. It has to be on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you help Ms. Carter then by answering the question. There's no secret about it now. It's a long time ago. How far were you from the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's really hard for me to say now, at least a kilometre away from the village, at least, because we didn't approach any closer since it would have been dangerous because of the armed terrorists that was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All I wanted was the distance roughly, that's all she wanted. She can ask you other questions once she gets the basic information. Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: The reason you're being asked these questions which is because in later orders which we'll discuss further on you indicate, such as on 4 April 1999 which is Exhibit 2813, it doesn't need to be pulled up right now; but you're talking about the command post in the time of introduction in the Grudic Mahala village in a school, the next command post will be in Vrbovac also in a school, there's others that indicate they were in factories and other positions. So how are you selecting if these are near villages -- there are other times that you're directly in a village, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Carter, if that's what it says here, it doesn't mean I was there, but if there was a living person in that village then we weren't there; if it's a school, it can only be an abandoned school, an old school, only that, by no means a school with students in it or pupils. So if there was a single person in a village, there was no command post in the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And to follow-up on something that you discussed on direct examination, wouldn't it be fair to say with items such as the Feronikel factory and other items, at the point the VJ starts using schools, factories, or any other civilian building as a command post or other military usages, then they become legitimate targets, do they not?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: No, unfortunately in this case you're wrong. I have to tell you, I do apologise. In Feronikel, there was no so much as a military boot let alone a soldier or military equipment, and yet it was targeted. Why it was declared to be a legitimate target, I don't know. All I know is we were not in Feronikel. Ms. Carter, would we enter Feronikel, this huge facility, and stay there waiting there to be targeted? No. We were in a safe place, certainly not in Feronikel.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: There has been evidence that contradicts you, however, we will move on and go back to the original operation on 22 March. Can you please on the screen mark for us where your brigade set up in order to produce this operation.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Carter, please give me the report and I'll mark it there. A long time has elapsed in the meantime --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: -- and without the report I can't mark this.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, P2031 is the order we're discussing, it is in front of you.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA DIKOVIC
utterances.text: What date did you mention, sorry?
